items.title: The Adoration of the Magi
items.artist: Fra Angelico and Fra Filippo Lippi
items.line: The Magi kneel before the Christ Child in a round panel.
items.explanation: The three Magi kneel before the Infant Jesus on Mary's lap, while a long procession winds down from the city behind them. Peacocks on the stable roof stand for immortality, and the half-ruined building recalls the old order giving way to Christ. Fra Angelico began the panel and Fra Filippo Lippi completed it.

credit.author: Fra Angelico and Fra Filippo Lippi

items.title: Adoration of the Magi (Strozzi Altarpiece)
items.line: Kings, horses and courtiers crowd towards the newborn Christ.
items.explanation: The three kings arrive at Bethlehem in the splendour of a Florentine court, with gold leaf and raised gilding on their crowns and robes. The eldest king kneels and kisses the Child's foot, the second removes his crown, and the youngest waits his turn. Small scenes above show the star, the journey and the arrival at Jerusalem.

items.title: Mystic Nativity
items.line: Angels dance in a ring above the stable at Bethlehem.
items.explanation: Mary kneels before the Child in a rocky stable, with St Joseph asleep beside her. Above, twelve angels dance in a circle holding olive branches; below, angels embrace men while small devils flee into the rocks. Botticelli's Greek inscription at the top links the scene with the Book of the Apocalypse.

items.title: The Nativity (Scrovegni Chapel fresco)
items.line: Mary turns towards her newborn Son in a simple shed.
items.explanation: Mary lies on a rocky ledge and takes the swaddled Child from a helper, while St Joseph sits apart, deep in thought. Angels gather above the roof and one turns to tell the shepherds, who stand at the right with their flock. The ox and the ass look on, recalling Isaiah 1:3.

items.title: The Adoration of the Shepherds
items.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
items.line: Shepherds kneel in a sunlit landscape before the Child.
items.explanation: Mary kneels in prayer over the Child, who lies on her blue mantle, and St Joseph sleeps on the left. Two shepherds in rough clothes and bare feet approach in reverence. The broken fence and the wide river valley give the scene the clear light and sharp detail for which Mantegna is known.

items.title: The Rest on the Flight into Egypt
items.line: The Holy Family rests on the road to Egypt.
items.explanation: Mary sits with the Child in a quiet Flemish landscape during the flight into Egypt. The Child holds a bunch of grapes, a sign of the Eucharist. Behind them the road winds away through woods towards a distant city.

items.title: The Holy Family with a Little Bird
items.line: The Child Jesus plays with a bird while St Joseph watches.
items.explanation: The Holy Family appears in an ordinary Spanish home. The Child holds up a small bird out of reach of a white dog, as St Joseph smiles and Mary pauses from winding thread. The carpenter's bench and tools on the floor show the hidden life at Nazareth.

items.title: Christ in the House of His Parents
items.line: In the carpenter's shop, the Boy Jesus has cut his hand.
items.explanation: The Boy Jesus has wounded his palm on a nail, and a drop of blood has fallen on his foot, foreshadowing the Crucifixion. Mary kneels to comfort him, while the young John the Baptist brings water in a bowl. The ladder, the dove and the flock outside the door are further signs of the Passion, the Holy Spirit and the Church.

items.title: The Baptism of Christ
items.line: John pours water over Christ as the Holy Spirit descends.
items.explanation: Christ stands in the Jordan while John the Baptist pours water over his head and the Holy Spirit descends as a white dove. Three angels stand under a walnut tree at the left, and a man undresses for baptism behind. The calm light and clear geometry are typical of Piero della Francesca.

items.title: The Baptism of Christ
items.artist: Andrea del Verrocchio and Leonardo da Vinci
items.line: Christ is baptised; the young Leonardo painted one angel.
items.explanation: John the Baptist baptises Christ in the Jordan as the dove of the Holy Spirit descends and the hands of God the Father appear above. Two angels kneel at the left holding Christ's garments. The angel on the far left is traditionally given to the young Leonardo da Vinci, then an apprentice in Verrocchio's workshop.

items.title: The Raising of Lazarus
items.place: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
items.line: Christ calls Lazarus out of the tomb.
items.explanation: Christ raises his hand over the open tomb at Bethany, and Lazarus rises from the grave, still pale in death. Martha and Mary start back in astonishment. Lazarus's sword and quiver hang on the wall of the tomb above.

items.title: The Wedding at Cana
items.line: Christ turns water into wine at a vast Venetian feast.
items.explanation: Christ sits at the centre of the wedding feast at Cana, with Mary beside him, as servants pour out the water that has become wine (John 2:1-11). More than a hundred guests fill the scene in sixteenth-century dress. The painting is almost ten metres wide and was made for the refectory of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice.

items.title: The Miraculous Draught of Fishes (tapestry cartoon)
items.place: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Royal Collection loan)
items.line: Peter kneels before Christ after the great catch of fish.
items.explanation: After a night of catching nothing, Peter and the other fishermen let down their nets at Christ's word and fill two boats (Luke 5:1-11). Peter kneels before Christ in the boat, saying, Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. Raphael designed it as a full-size cartoon for a tapestry in the Sistine Chapel.

items.title: The Sermon on the Mount
items.line: Christ teaches the crowd on the mountain.
items.explanation: Christ sits on the hillside and teaches the Beatitudes to the people gathered round him (Matthew 5-7). Listeners of every age lean in, some intent, some troubled, some at peace. Carl Bloch painted it for the chapel of Frederiksborg Castle in Denmark.

items.title: The Transfiguration
items.line: Christ shines on Mount Tabor above a scene of need below.
items.explanation: Christ rises in glory between Moses and Elijah, while Peter, James and John fall dazzled on the mountain. Below, the other Apostles cannot heal a boy possessed by a spirit, and the crowd points up to the only One who can (Matthew 17). It was Raphael's last painting and was carried at his funeral.

items.title: The Last Supper
items.line: Christ tells the Twelve that one of them will betray him.
items.explanation: Christ has just said, One of you will betray me, and the Apostles react in groups of three. Judas, clutching the money bag, leans back into shadow, while John leans towards Peter. Christ sits at the centre against the window, his hands open towards the bread and the wine.

items.title: The Last Supper
items.line: Christ gives Communion at a table lit by angels.
items.explanation: The table runs diagonally into the room, and Christ, haloed in light, gives the bread to an Apostle. Servants work on in the foreground and angels gather in the smoke of the lamp above. Judas sits alone on the near side of the table.

items.title: The Agony in the Garden
items.line: Christ prays in the garden as the Apostles sleep.
items.explanation: Christ kneels on a rock in Gethsemane while Peter, James and John sleep below. Angels show him the instruments of his Passion, and Judas leads the soldiers out of Jerusalem along the road.

items.title: Christ Carrying the Cross
items.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
items.line: Christ embraces the Cross and looks up to heaven.
items.explanation: Christ carries the Cross alone, holding it gently, his eyes raised to heaven. The crown of thorns presses on his head, but his face is calm. El Greco and his workshop painted this subject many times for private devotion.

items.title: Christ Crucified
items.line: Christ hangs alone on the Cross against a dark ground.
items.explanation: Christ hangs dead on the Cross with nothing around him but darkness. He is fixed with four nails, as Velázquez's teacher Francisco Pacheco advised, and the title above is written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Velázquez painted it for the Benedictine convent of San Plácido in Madrid.

items.title: The Crucifixion (Calvary)
items.place: Royal Museum of Fine Arts, Antwerp
items.line: Christ is crucified between the two thieves.
items.explanation: Christ hangs between the two thieves, whose bodies twist on rough tree trunks. Mary sits grieving at the foot of the Cross and St John kneels in prayer. Skulls and bones on the ground recall that Calvary was the place of the skull.

items.title: The Descent from the Cross
items.line: Christ's body is lowered from the Cross.
items.explanation: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lower the body of Christ, while Mary collapses in a pose that mirrors her Son's. St John supports her, and St Mary Magdalene wrings her hands at the right. The figures are set in a shallow gilded box, like carved statues in an altarpiece.

items.title: The Lamentation (Scrovegni Chapel fresco)
items.line: Mary holds her dead Son as angels weep in the sky.
items.explanation: Mary cradles the head of her dead Son, while St John flings his arms back in grief and St Mary Magdalene holds Christ's feet. Ten angels cry out in the blue sky above. The bare tree on the rock may stand for the Tree of Knowledge, and for life that will return.

items.title: The Entombment of Christ
items.line: Christ's body is laid on the stone of anointing.
items.explanation: Nicodemus and St John lower the body of Christ onto the stone slab. Behind them stand Mary, St Mary Magdalene and Mary of Clopas, the last raising her arms to heaven. The corner of the stone projects towards the viewer, as if over the altar where the painting first hung.

items.title: The Resurrection
items.line: The risen Christ steps out of the tomb as the soldiers sleep.
items.explanation: Christ rises from the tomb holding the banner of the Resurrection, one foot on the edge of the sarcophagus. Four soldiers sleep below. The trees on the left are bare and those on the right are in leaf, showing new life after death.

items.title: Supper at Emmaus
items.line: The risen Christ is recognised in the breaking of bread.
items.explanation: At Emmaus, two disciples recognise the risen Christ as he blesses the bread (Luke 24:30-31). One pushes back his chair and the other flings out his arms, while the innkeeper looks on, unaware. The basket of fruit seems to tip over the edge of the table into the viewer's space.

items.title: The Ascension (Scrovegni Chapel fresco)
items.line: Christ ascends into heaven before Mary and the Apostles.
items.explanation: Christ rises into heaven with his hands stretched upwards, surrounded by the souls of the just. Below, Mary and the Apostles kneel on either side, and two angels in white tell them that he will return (Acts 1:11). The fresco is part of Giotto's cycle in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua.

items.title: The Sacred Heart of Jesus
items.line: The Sacred Heart of Jesus.
items.explanation: Christ holds out his Heart, crowned with thorns, burning with flames and topped by a cross. The painting was made for the Church of the Gesù in Rome and became the model for countless images of the Sacred Heart. It reflects the devotion that grew after the appearances to St Margaret Mary Alacoque.

items.title: Christ Pantocrator (icon)
items.line: The oldest known icon of Christ Pantocrator.
items.explanation: Christ looks out from a gold ground, blessing with his right hand and holding the Gospels in his left. The two sides of his face differ slightly, often read as his divine and human natures. The icon was painted in encaustic wax and has been kept at St Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai since the sixth century.

items.title: Christ Pantocrator (Deësis mosaic)
items.line: Christ between Mary and St John the Baptist.
items.explanation: Christ is shown as Judge and Saviour, with Mary and St John the Baptist on either side asking mercy for mankind; this grouping is called the Deësis. The mosaic, made of small glass and gold tesserae, survives in the upper gallery of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul. The faces are among the finest in Byzantine art.

items.title: Christ Pantocrator (apse mosaic)
items.line: Christ Pantocrator fills the apse at Cefalù.
items.explanation: Christ fills the apse with his right hand raised in blessing and the open Gospel in his left, reading in Greek and Latin: I am the light of the world (John 8:12). Below him stand Mary, archangels and the Apostles. The mosaic was made for the Norman king Roger II of Sicily.

items.title: Salvator Mundi
items.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
items.line: Christ as Saviour of the World, holding the globe.
items.explanation: Christ raises his right hand in blessing and holds the orb of the world, crowned by a cross. Dürer left the painting unfinished, so the underdrawing shows through in the robe. The subject, Salvator Mundi, means Saviour of the World.

items.title: The Annunciation
items.line: The Annunciation, with Adam and Eve leaving Eden.
items.explanation: The Archangel Gabriel greets Mary in a loggia, and a ray of light carries the dove of the Holy Spirit to her. On the left, an angel drives Adam and Eve out of Eden: the first Eve brought sin, and Mary's yes brings the Saviour. The small scenes below show her life.

items.title: The Annunciation (north corridor fresco)
items.line: Gabriel and Mary in the quiet of the friary at San Marco.
items.explanation: The Archangel Gabriel bows before Mary, who sits on a simple stool in a bare cloister. Fra Angelico painted it at the top of the stairs in the Dominican friary of San Marco, Florence. The inscription asked each friar to say a Hail Mary as he passed.

items.title: The Annunciation with St Margaret and St Ansanus
items.line: Gabriel greets Mary with an olive branch on a gold ground.
items.explanation: Gabriel kneels with an olive branch, and the words of his greeting run in raised gold from his lips: Ave gratia plena Dominus tecum. Mary draws back, her book closed on her thumb. The lilies in the vase stand for her purity.

items.title: The Annunciation
items.line: The Annunciation in a church, with Mary as the new Temple.
items.explanation: Gabriel greets Mary inside a tall church, the words of the greeting written on the panel, and her reply written upside down for God to read. The rounded windows above and the pointed ones below suggest the passage from the Old Covenant to the New. The lilies and the dove complete the scene.

items.title: The Visitation
items.line: Mary and Elizabeth embrace.
items.explanation: Mary, newly with child, meets her cousin Elizabeth, who kneels before her (Luke 1:39-56). Elizabeth's child leaps in her womb, and she greets Mary as the mother of my Lord. Two women stand beside them in the street of a Renaissance town.

items.title: The Visitation
items.line: Mary and Elizabeth meet, watched by two women.
items.explanation: Mary and Elizabeth embrace, their faces almost touching, while two women look straight out at the viewer. The bright, sharp colours are typical of Pontormo. The altarpiece hangs in the parish church of San Michele at Carmignano, near Florence.

items.title: The Birth of the Virgin (Scrovegni Chapel fresco)
items.line: St Anne gives birth to Mary.
items.explanation: St Anne lies in bed and receives the newborn Mary from a midwife, while women bring linen and water. The scene comes from the life of Mary told in the ancient Protoevangelium of James. It is part of Giotto's fresco cycle in the Scrovegni Chapel.

items.title: The Sistine Madonna
items.line: Mary appears in the clouds with the Child.
items.explanation: Mary walks forward on the clouds holding the Child, between St Sixtus and St Barbara, as curtains part on a heaven full of angels' faces. Two small cherubs lean on the ledge at the bottom. Raphael painted it for the monks of San Sisto in Piacenza.

items.title: Madonna of the Goldfinch
items.line: The Child Jesus strokes a goldfinch.
items.explanation: Mary sits in a meadow with the Child Jesus, who strokes a goldfinch held by the young St John the Baptist. The goldfinch, which eats thistles, was a sign of the Passion. The panel broke into pieces when the owner's house collapsed in 1547, and was pieced back together.

items.title: Madonna of the Magnificat
items.line: Mary writes the Magnificat as angels crown her.
items.explanation: Mary writes the opening words of her hymn, My soul doth magnify the Lord (Luke 1:46-55), in a book held by angels, as two more crown her Queen of Heaven. The Child guides her hand and holds a pomegranate, a sign of the Resurrection. The round painting is called a tondo.

items.title: Madonna and Child with Two Angels
items.line: Mary prays as two angels lift up the Child.
items.explanation: Mary sits in prayer at a window, wearing a fine veil, as two angels hold up the Child towards her. One angel turns and smiles at the viewer. The landscape behind opens towards a far-off city and sea.

items.title: The Madonna of Chancellor Rolin
items.line: The Chancellor kneels before Mary and the Child.
items.explanation: Nicolas Rolin, Chancellor of Burgundy, kneels at his prayer book before Mary, who is about to be crowned by an angel. The Child blesses him. Through the arches a river city stretches into the distance, painted in minute detail.

items.title: The Pietà of Villeneuve-lès-Avignon
items.line: Mary holds her dead Son across her knees.
items.explanation: Mary holds the body of Christ across her knees, with St John removing the crown of thorns and St Mary Magdalene holding the ointment jar. A kneeling canon prays at the left. The gold ground and the distant city of Jerusalem set the scene outside time.

items.title: The Assumption of the Virgin (Assunta)
items.line: Mary is taken up into heaven before the Apostles.
items.explanation: Mary rises on a cloud towards God the Father, her arms raised, while the Apostles reach up in wonder below. The painting, almost seven metres tall, stands over the high altar of the Frari church in Venice. Its strong reds draw the eye up from earth to heaven.

items.title: The Assumption of the Virgin
items.line: Mary rises from the empty tomb as the Apostles look on.
items.explanation: The Apostles and the holy women gather at Mary's tomb and find only roses and her burial cloth, as she is borne up by angels. Rubens painted it for the high altar of the Cathedral of Our Lady in Antwerp. It belongs to the same church as his Descent from the Cross.

items.title: The Coronation of the Virgin (detail)
items.line: Mary is crowned Queen of Heaven among the Saints.
items.explanation: God the Father crowns Mary among a crowd of angels and Saints holding lilies. Fra Filippo Lippi painted himself among them, at the left, looking out. The painting was made for the convent of Sant'Ambrogio in Florence.

items.title: The Immaculate Conception of El Escorial
items.line: Mary as the Immaculate Conception, borne up by angels.
items.explanation: Mary stands on the crescent moon, lifted by angels, her hands crossed on her breast and her eyes raised to heaven. She is dressed in white and blue, colours tied to the Immaculate Conception. The image echoes the woman clothed with the sun in Apocalypse 12.

items.title: The Immaculate Conception
items.place: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya, Barcelona
items.line: Mary as the Immaculate Conception, with the city below.
items.explanation: Mary stands on the moon against a golden sky, her hands joined in prayer. Below lies a calm landscape with a city. Zurbarán painted many such images for Spanish churches.

items.title: The Immaculate Conception
items.line: Mary as the Immaculate Conception, stars round her head.
items.explanation: Mary stands on the moon with twelve stars round her head and the sun behind her, as in Apocalypse 12:1. The young Velázquez painted it in Seville, where the doctrine was deeply loved long before it was defined in 1854. Symbols of the litany appear in the landscape below.

items.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe (the original tilma image)
items.place: Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mexico City
items.line: Our Lady of Guadalupe, on Juan Diego's tilma.
items.explanation: This is the image that appeared on the cloak of St Juan Diego in December 1531, at Tepeyac near Mexico City. Mary stands before the sun, on the moon, with her hands joined, her mantle covered with stars and a black band at her waist, the sign of a woman with child. The cloth is kept in the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe.

items.title: Salus Populi Romani (icon)
items.place: Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, Rome
items.line: Salus Populi Romani, the ancient icon of Rome.
items.explanation: Mary holds the Child, who blesses and holds a book, while she crosses her hands with a small cloth. The icon is kept in the Basilica of St Mary Major in Rome. It has been carried through the city in times of plague, and Popes have prayed before it for centuries.

items.title: Our Lady of Częstochowa (the Black Madonna, without its metal cover)
items.line: Our Lady of Częstochowa, Queen of Poland.
items.explanation: Mary points to the Child she holds, as the One who is the Way, and the Child blesses with his right hand. Two scars on her cheek are traditionally said to come from an attack in 1430. The icon is kept at the Jasna Góra Monastery in Poland.

items.title: Our Lady of Vladimir (icon)
items.line: Our Lady of Vladimir, the Mother of Tenderness.
items.explanation: The Child presses his cheek against his Mother's, and she looks out with sorrow, knowing what is to come. This type of icon is called Eleousa, the Virgin of Tenderness. It was painted in Constantinople and brought to Kyiv and then to Vladimir and Moscow.

items.title: The Last Judgement
items.line: Christ judges the living and the dead.
items.explanation: Christ sits in judgement among the angels and Saints, with the open tombs in a long line below. On his right, the blessed dance with angels in a garden towards the gates of heaven; on his left, the damned are driven into hell. Fra Angelico painted it for the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli in Florence.

items.title: The Crucifixion; The Last Judgment
items.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
items.line: The Crucifixion and the Last Judgement, side by side.
items.explanation: The left panel shows Calvary crowded with people, with Mary and St John grieving in the foreground. The right panel shows the Last Judgement: Christ above, the Archangel Michael standing on a skeleton in the centre, and the damned falling into hell below. The frames carry texts from Scripture.

items.title: The Last Judgement
items.line: The Last Judgement on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel.
items.explanation: Christ raises his arm in judgement at the centre, with Mary close at his side. The Saints gather round holding the signs of their martyrdom, the dead rise from their graves below, and Charon ferries the damned across. Michelangelo painted it over the altar of the Sistine Chapel.

items.title: The Last Judgement (Scrovegni Chapel fresco)
items.line: Christ the Judge, with heaven and hell on either side.
items.explanation: Christ sits in a rainbow mandorla with the Apostles enthroned on either side. On his right the blessed rise in order; on his left rivers of fire carry the damned to hell. Below the cross, Enrico Scrovegni offers the chapel to Mary.

items.title: The Beaune Altarpiece (The Last Judgement)
items.line: St Michael weighs souls before Christ the Judge.
items.explanation: Christ sits on a rainbow, a lily on one side for mercy and a sword on the other for justice. Below him the Archangel Michael weighs souls, and the dead rise to heaven or hell. Rogier van der Weyden painted it for the hospital chapel of the Hôtel-Dieu in Beaune.

items.title: The Last Judgement triptych
items.line: Bosch's vision of the end of the world.
items.explanation: Christ sits in judgement above, while below the earth is filled with strange creatures tormenting sinners. The left wing shows the Fall and Paradise, and the right wing shows hell. The triptych warns against each of the deadly sins.

items.title: The Ghent Altarpiece (open), with the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb
items.line: The Adoration of the Lamb: the whole Church before God.
items.explanation: At the centre of the Ghent Altarpiece, the Lamb of God stands on the altar, his blood flowing into a chalice, with the dove of the Holy Spirit above and the Fountain of Life below (Apocalypse 7 and 22). Prophets, Apostles, martyrs, virgins and pilgrims come from every side to adore him. Above sit God, Mary and St John the Baptist.

items.title: Christ Glorified in the Court of Heaven
items.line: Christ in glory among the whole court of heaven.
items.explanation: Christ stands in glory at the centre, holding the banner of the Resurrection, surrounded by angels playing music. On either side hundreds of Saints, each with a name and sign, stand in rows. It was the predella of the high altarpiece of San Domenico at Fiesole.

items.title: Paradise
items.line: Paradise, the largest canvas of its age.
items.explanation: Christ and Mary sit at the centre of heaven, surrounded by circles of angels and Saints that stretch outwards in every direction. The canvas, more than twenty metres wide, fills the end wall of the Great Council Hall in the Doge's Palace, Venice. Tintoretto completed it with his son Domenico.

items.title: The Fall of the Rebel Angels
items.place: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels
items.line: St Michael casts out the rebel angels.
items.explanation: The Archangel Michael, in gold armour, and his angels drive Lucifer and the rebel angels out of heaven (Apocalypse 12:7-9). As they fall, the rebels turn into strange creatures, part fish, part insect, part bird. Bruegel painted it in 1562, and it is in Brussels.
